label: lf-green-retardants
topic: Bio-based flame-retardant coatings on wood, textiles and bio-composites: reported fire-test numbers, and what the FireCoatingCertificate.lean bounds can eliminate or keep
summary:
Harvested 16 papers with reported fire numbers; all 17 DOIs (16 papers plus one preprint) redirect at doi.org (HTTP 302). Every number comes from the Europe PMC abstract record, read through a summarising fetch tool, not from full texts, so the quotes are tool-extracted and need a spot check before reuse.

Coverage is uneven. Peak-HRR reduction and LOI are well covered. Time to ignition appears in one paper only (32 to 69 s). Char yield appears in one paper only (23.80% to 38.10%). No paper with numbers was found for casein or DNA coatings, and the mineral/clay entry is an impregnation, not a surface coating.

What the Lean bounds can do with these numbers:
- **Nothing is eliminated outright.** No abstract gives coating thickness, conductivity, char thickness, heat flux or burn duration, which are the hypotheses the certificates need.
- **LOI claims are out of scope.** The file has no oxygen or gas-phase theorem, so LOI values can be neither eliminated nor kept.
- **Back-face insulation (sections 1-2):** thin layer-by-layer films would add almost no d/k, so `steady_eliminates` would rule them out as insulators unless a char term (`char_eliminates`, needs xmax and kcmin) rescues them. This is my reasoning from typical film thicknesses, not from a sourced thickness.
- **Ignition (section 5):** the one time-to-ignition claim (hydrogel/MXene on wood, 32 to 69 s) is kept, not eliminated. A coating that is 90% water or more plausibly raises thermal inertia enough, and evaporation is outside the no-loss model anyway. For thin fabrics, `thin_ignition_eliminates` caps ignition delay by areal heat capacity, so a large delay claimed for a light coating on cotton would be eliminable; none of these abstracts makes such a claim.
- **Peak HRR (section 6, `hrr_eliminates`):** this is the only bound I could apply numerically. For the chitosan/graphene oxide/APP coating on wood, THR divided by HRR gives a minimum burn window of about 597 s coated (34.31 MJ/m2 over 57.51 kW/m2) and 592 s uncoated (62.43 over 105.50). The claim survives only if the test burned at least about 10 minutes. For the cotton paper reporting pHRR down 87.7% and THR down 63.7%, the minimum burn window must grow about 2.95 times relative to untreated; this is checkable against the HRR curve.
- **Reductions where THR falls at least as much as the peak** (44.1/55.4, 25/54, 77/75, 67/80) impose no extra burn-time demand and are kept trivially.

The only file I wrote is the DOI resolution log for the second batch, at D:/Users/ashenoy00000/delphi-work/agents4/lf-green-retardants/doi_resolution_batch2.txt. The time limit ran out before I wrote a findings data file.

findings.claim: Applying hrr_eliminates (peak >= energy / burn time) to the Yan 2022 wood numbers: the coated sample needs a burn window of at least about 597 s and the uncoated at least about 592 s. The claim is consistent only if the cone test burned for about 10 minutes or more; a shorter reported burn would eliminate it.
findings.confidence: medium: arithmetic checked; assumes the abstract's 'heat release rate' is the peak and that all fuel energy is in THR; burn duration not in the abstract

findings.claim: Applying the same bound to Li P 2026 (pHRR -87.7%, THR -63.7%): the minimum burn window (THR/pHRR) must be about 2.95 times that of untreated cotton. This is a testable consequence against the published HRR curve, not an elimination.
findings.confidence: medium: arithmetic checked; needs the HRR curve from the full text to decide

findings.claim: No candidate can be formally eliminated from abstract-level data. The certificates need coating thickness and conductivity envelopes (steady_eliminates), char thickness and conductivity (char_eliminates), thermal inertia and imposed flux (thick/thin_ignition_eliminates) or fuel mass and burn time (hrr_eliminates), none of which the abstracts report. LOI claims are outside the file's scope entirely.
findings.confidence: high for the scope statement (file read in full to line 299); the hypotheses needed are those in the theorem statements

findings.claim: The single time-to-ignition claim (hydrogel coating, 32 to 69 s) is kept rather than eliminated: tigThick scales linearly with thermal inertia, and a coating that is mostly water plausibly more than doubles surface inertia; evaporation is also outside the no-loss model, which only makes ignition later.
findings.confidence: low-medium: qualitative argument from general material properties, no sourced kρc values and no heat flux in the abstract

key_claims: 16 papers harvested with reported fire numbers; all 17 DOIs (including one preprint) redirect at doi.org.
All numbers are abstract-level, read from Europe PMC records through a summarising tool; no full text was opened.
Time to ignition was found in one paper (32 to 69 s) and char yield in one paper (23.80% to 38.10%).
No abstract supplies the inputs needed for a formal elimination under FireCoatingCertificate.lean; LOI is outside its scope.
The fuel-load bound gives two checkable consequences: a burn window of about 10 minutes for the Yan 2022 wood coating, and a 2.95-fold longer minimum burn window for the Li 2026 cotton coating.
Thin layer-by-layer films would fail any back-face insulation criterion unless their char layer supplies the resistance; this is reasoning, not a sourced result.
could_not_find: Any paper with quantitative fire numbers for a casein coating (search returned none)
Any paper with quantitative fire numbers for a DNA coating (search returned none)
A mineral/clay surface nanocoating with numbers; the only clay entry is a montmorillonite impregnation of poplar
Tannin as the main flame retardant; tannic acid appears only as a curing agent in one resin coating
Time-to-ignition numbers beyond one paper; char-yield numbers beyond one paper
Coating thickness, thermal conductivity, char thickness, cone heat flux or burn duration for any paper (not in abstracts)
Full texts: none were opened, so no number was checked against a table or figure
Carosio et al. 2012 (Carbohydrate Polymers) appeared in the search but its abstract gives time to ignition only qualitatively; not used
Which two quantities fell by 89.3% and 49.3% in Shi H 2024
recommendations: Open the full texts of the three open-access papers (Sci Rep 10.1038/s41598-023-28228-5, ACS Omega 10.1021/acsomega.2c03624, Front Chem 10.3389/fchem.2024.1503694) to get heat flux, burn duration and coating thickness, then instantiate hrr_eliminates and thick_ignition_eliminates with real numbers.
Check the Yan 2022 HRR curve: if flaming ended well before about 590 s, the reported HRR/THR pair is inconsistent with the energy bound.
Check the Li P 2026 HRR curve for the roughly threefold longer burn the bound requires.
Resolve the Wang Y 2023 percentage (17.5% stated, about 14.9% from the two values) against the full text before quoting it.
Run separate searches for casein, DNA and clay nanocoatings in a database with better coverage of Polymer Degradation and Stability and ACS Nano; Europe PMC abstract search returned nothing for them.
Spot-check each quote against the publisher abstract before any nanopublication, since the quotes were extracted by a summarising tool.
lay_summary: Scientists are making fire-protecting coatings for wood and cloth out of natural things like plant acids, shellfish shells and seaweed.
I collected 16 studies and wrote down how much each coating cut the fire's strongest heat, usually by a fifth up to almost nine tenths.
I only read the short summaries of the studies, not the whole papers, so the numbers still need a second check.
The project's maths rules can throw out a coating only when they know how thick it is and how long the fire test burned, and the summaries do not say that.
So nothing was thrown out yet, but the maths did give two simple checks, such as 'this wood test must have burned for about ten minutes'.

glossary.cone calorimeter: A lab machine that heats a small sample with a cone-shaped heater and measures how much heat it gives off as it burns.
glossary.HRR (heat release rate): How fast a burning sample gives off heat, in kilowatts per square metre.
glossary.pHRR (peak heat release rate): The highest heat release rate reached during the test.
glossary.THR (total heat release): All the heat given off over the whole test, in megajoules per square metre.
glossary.TSP (total smoke production): All the smoke given off over the whole test.
glossary.LOI (limiting oxygen index): The smallest percentage of oxygen in the surrounding gas that keeps the sample burning; higher means harder to burn.
glossary.time to ignition (TTI): How many seconds the heated sample takes to catch fire.
glossary.char yield / char residue: The share of the sample left as black carbon crust after burning.
glossary.UL-94 V0: The best grade in a standard small-flame test; the sample stops burning quickly without dripping flames.
glossary.layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly: Building a coating by dipping the material alternately in two solutions that stick to each other, one thin layer at a time.
glossary.bilayer (BL): One pair of layers in a layer-by-layer coating.
glossary.phytic acid: A phosphorus-rich acid found in seeds and grains.
glossary.chitosan: A substance made from the shells of shrimp and crabs.
glossary.lignin: The stiff natural glue in wood.
glossary.tannic acid: A plant substance found in bark and tea.
glossary.montmorillonite: A kind of clay made of very thin plates.
glossary.MXene: A man-made material of very thin metal-carbide sheets.
glossary.graphene oxide: Very thin sheets of carbon with oxygen attached.
glossary.hydrogel: A soft solid that is mostly water held in a network.
glossary.impregnation: Soaking a treatment into the body of the wood instead of painting it on the surface.
glossary.delignified wood: Wood with its lignin removed, leaving a porous cellulose frame.
glossary.intumescent: Swelling into a thick foam-like char when heated.
glossary.thermal conductivity (k): How easily heat flows through a material.
glossary.thermal resistance (d/k): How strongly a layer of thickness d blocks heat flow.
glossary.thermal inertia (kρc): How slowly a surface heats up; the product of conductivity, density and heat capacity.
glossary.back-face temperature rise: How much hotter the side away from the fire becomes.
glossary.thermally thin / thick: Thin means the whole sample heats evenly; thick means the far side has not yet felt the heat.
glossary.heat flux: Heat energy arriving per square metre per second.
glossary.fuel load: The amount of burnable material per unit area.
glossary.elimination certificate: A proof that a candidate must fail a stated test under stated assumptions; it can rule out but never approve.
glossary.DOI: A permanent identifier for a published paper.
glossary.Europe PMC: A free online index of research paper records and abstracts.
